grammar.title: Inversion After Negative Adverbials
grammar.explanation:
When a sentence **starts** with a negative or limiting word, such as **never**, **rarely**, **hardly**, **not only** or **only when**, we use **question word order** — auxiliary verb before the subject. ***Never have I** seen such a beautiful view.*

This is called **inversion**. It is formal and emphatic, and it is common in writing, speeches and storytelling. It makes a sentence sound stronger and more dramatic.

If there is no auxiliary verb, add **do**, **does** or **did**. We rarely see talent like this becomes **Rarely do we** see talent like this. With **be**, just put **be** first: **Not only was he** late.

**Hardly** and **scarcely** go with **when**, and **no sooner** goes with **than**. **Hardly had** we arrived **when** it started to rain. **No sooner had** she left **than** he arrived. Do not mix them.

**Not only** goes with **but (also)**. **Not only does** she speak French, **but** she also speaks Arabic. The inversion is in the first part, and **but** introduces the second part.

With **only when**, **only after**, **only then** and **not until**, the inversion is in the **main clause**. **Only when** I got home **did I** realise. **Not until** the end **did we** find out the truth.

Strong negative phrases also trigger inversion: **under no circumstances**, **on no account**, **at no time**, **in no way**. **Under no circumstances should** you open this door. **Little** means not at all: **Little did** I know that my life was about to change.

A common mistake is to keep normal word order after the negative word. *Never I have seen* is wrong. Say **Never have I** seen. And never put **would** in the wrong place: the auxiliary must come before the subject.
examples: ***Never have I** felt so proud.* (never + present perfect)
***Seldom has** the city looked so beautiful.* (seldom)
***No sooner had** she left **than** he arrived.* (no sooner… than)
***Not only is** the hotel cheap, **but** it's also very comfortable.* (not only… but)
***Not until** I got home **did I** notice the missing wallet.* (not until)
***Little did** they know that we were watching.* (little = not at all)
